pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

## 598adf58-4d0d-4866-82b2-42a10512e240

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. # Applications: The Missing Variable (Kraus, SSAC26)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Women's sport teams at Baylor could add a low-burden symptom log (cycle day, bleed pattern, symptoms) to the existing athlete-monitoring intake, owned jointly by Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance, matching the speaker's "start with symptom tracking" step [16:46].
- Inference: When a female athlete has a bone stress injury or a missed-period history, Athletic Medicine and Performance Nutrition could be asked whether low energy availability was screened before the load history is reviewed. The speaker links low energy availability, suppressed estrogen and bone stress injury [13:38].
- Inference: Any roster-wide load or jump-testing report (for example CMJ output on ForceDecks) could carry a flag for "individual outlier versus her own baseline" instead of a team or calendar-phase cutoff, because the speaker says average phase effects are small but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- Inference: The data-privacy question raised in Q&A [26:12] applies directly to anything Applied Performance stores in Kitman Labs: decide who can see cycle data before collecting any.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use after about a year because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers, but they are deliberately kept for return-to-play and chronic-condition cases where subjective context adds value (SportSmith piece on the ER/wellness experiment). The talk partly conflicts and partly extends: the speaker wants symptom tracking [16:46] and admits that if fewer than about half of athletes actually collect data it may not be worth it [19:29], which is the same compliance concern Eric named. It extends his keep-it-for-selected-cases rule: a cycle log could be a targeted, opt-in tool rather than a daily roster survey.
- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight; stop when insight no longer justifies the cost. The talk agrees on the cost side (testing is invasive, expensive or needs validation [15:42]) and does not show the insight side.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to him. The speaker's slogan that predictable injuries are preventable [05:51] is stronger than Eric's stance; she also says there is no conclusive evidence on hormone levels and ACL risk [10:32].
- Eric's baseline: Performance Nutrition owns nutrition and body composition, and Applied Performance supports Athletic Medicine's return-to-performance decisions. The talk's energy-availability material falls in those two units' lanes, so any use is a referral or shared-data question, not an Applied Performance decision.

## What would have to be true

- Athletic Medicine and Performance Nutrition agree on who owns a female-athlete screen and who sees the output.
- A collection method athletes will actually use (the speaker worries about 50% or less participation [20:01]); a pilot with volunteers in one sport would show this.
- A written data-access rule (athlete controls her data, not used to pull her from play [26:43]) approved before collection starts.
- Enough athletes with repeated cycles to see individual patterns; one season of one team is likely small.

## Do not apply when

- The plan is to adjust whole-team training by cycle phase. The speaker herself says the field is moving away from phase-based prescription [08:59].
- Calendar counting is the only data. She says it assumes a 28-day cycle and misses anovulation and luteal phase defects [15:12].
- The athlete is on hormonal contraception or has irregular bleeds and the method cannot tell what the hormones are doing [07:24].
- Football is the only population considered; the talk is about female athletes.
- Data could reach coaches in a way that affects playing time without the athlete's consent.

## First step

Ask the Athletic Medicine lead for women's sports whether any cycle or energy-availability screening already exists, and what consent and access rules cover it. No new collection until that is answered.

# Applications: Redefining Limits (SSAC26 panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Practice and warm-up design could include a planned constraint (for example a changed warm-up area, time or surface) for athletes who will face travel, TV or schedule disruptions. Magness describes taping off an area so an athlete must build a warm-up that works when the usual routine is not available [27:35].
- Inference: For a technique change on a veteran (sprint mechanics, for example), a constraint such as mini hurdles or barefoot running on a hard surface could be tested alongside verbal coaching. Magness describes Tom Tellez using both for an athlete who could not feel a drifting foot [29:06], [29:36].
- Inference: When a starter is injured, the staff could review how the rest of the lineup and its usage changed, using Epstein's description of a study where other players spread the ball and kept some of it after the star returned [22:31]. This is an observation to check in Baylor data, not a plan.
- Inference: Recovery could be scheduled the way training is. Epstein says he programmed volume but not recovery and improved when he cut one workout a week [07:13]. A check of whether weekly load and recovery days are both planned fits this.
- Inference: Reports to coaches could be judged by whether they lead to a change in the athlete or the drill, using Magness's point that the bottleneck is turning tracked data into something actionable [45:56].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters as much as any technology for daily assessment, and new movement patterns take about 3 to 4 weeks to become efficient (HHPR 5355 course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred in the baseline). The talk extends this: Magness says efficiency can numb feel, so athletes need the environment to change the pattern [28:36]; Battier says changing his shot took months [31:36].
- Eric's baseline: recovery has to be earned by training hard first, and recovery technology does not replace managing training stress. The talk is compatible but adds a different point: recovery must be planned, which Epstein says he neglected [07:13].
- Eric's baseline: favor a few valid, reliable tests tied to clear KPIs; data collection is judged on cost versus insight. The talk agrees with the insight side: Magness warns that biomarkers without a link to performance are the problem [46:28].
- Eric's baseline: a constraints-led approach is marked thin in his corpus. No stated position to compare; this talk is an outside source, not confirmation.
- Eric's baseline: Mental Health Services is a separate unit and Applied Performance supports collaboration with it. The panel's mental-tool material [02:38], [05:42] would be a referral or joint-planning topic, not an Applied Performance service.

## What would have to be true

- The coaches own the drill and agree to try a constraint for a defined block, with a stated measure (for example jump output, contact time or a coach rating).
- The athlete trusts the coach's reason. Magness's Carl Lewis example turns on that trust [33:38].
- A comparison condition exists: same athletes before and after, or a matched group.
- For the lineup observation, enough games with and without the starter to compare.

## Do not apply when

- The athlete is a novice; Magness says telling athletes how to do it worked sometimes, particularly with novices [29:36].
- The constraint adds injury risk (barefoot sprinting on a hard track, for example) without Athletic Medicine and sport coach agreement.
- In-season with no room to test; the panelists describe multi-month changes.
- The evidence is one panelist's anecdote (skeleton start, Sheila Taormina, Ryan Poles). These are stories, not tests.
- The athlete is a youth player; the panel notes youth sport decisions differ from pro development [11:48].

## First step

Pick one drill in one position group and write down, before using it, what the constraint blocks and what change you expect. Run it for two weeks and compare against the existing drill.

# Applications: Reimagining the NCAA (SSAC26 panel)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Applied Performance's own data store (Kitman Labs with Catapult, VALD and PFF feeds) has the same problem Stall describes: only three or four people can use the warehouse through code [28:03]. A natural-language question layer over cleaned data could let coaches ask their own questions, if accuracy can be checked.
- Inference: Stall's case for integrating a data source at low cost is a model for adding one new feed (for example a new wearable) after a manual pilot. He ran a year of manual imports by an intern, then measured revenue from those fans [09:45], [10:15].
- Inference: A standing weekly cross-staff meeting with current data at hand, so questions are answered in the room instead of after two weeks [28:33], could be tried between Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance.
- Inference: Stall's small-win approach (a simple change, like the team name in an email subject line [38:42]) applies to report design: pick one small, visible report change before building a large system.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Kitman Labs is the cross-technology data store and visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's reporting tool, and standardized weekly and monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist (Playbook and Development Plan). The talk agrees with the direction (shared data infrastructure, [41:16]) and extends it with the point that making data available across the organization is the opportunity [11:19].
- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight. Stall's intern pilot [10:15] is an example of measuring insight before paying for integration.
- Eric's baseline: the current data dictionary is organized by vendor and is hard for staff to use. The panel's point about democratizing data is consistent but does not address dictionary design.

## What would have to be true

- Data are cleaned and labeled before any AI question layer is used; Picaduro describes the human as staying in the loop [26:31].
- Athlete privacy rules exist for anything queried by non-specialists.
- A check that natural-language answers match the analyst's own query on a sample.
- A named owner for each feed.

## Do not apply when

- The idea is to copy ticket pricing or fan segmentation. Those are revenue functions, not Applied Performance.
- The source is one school's program (South Carolina's $20 million rise [20:26], 45% click-to-open gain [35:11], 35% sales gain [35:41]); the numbers are self-reported by panelists with commercial interests and come without a method, so they do not transfer as effect sizes.
- Athlete data would be sent to a third-party AI vendor without a review of Baylor's data rules.
- The data problem is data quality rather than access; better tooling will not fix that.

## First step

List every question a coach asked Applied Performance in the past month, how long each took to answer, and which could have been answered by a saved query. That shows whether an access problem exists here.

=== FILE: videos/2026-04-09_nRoPOxRWCaQ_the-missing-variable-menstrual-cycles-injury-risk-and-the-co/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: nRoPOxRWCaQ
title: "SSAC26: The Missing Variable: Menstrual Cycles, Injury Risk, and the Competitive Edge"
event: SSAC26 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Emily Kraus]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

Emily Kraus, a sports medicine physician, argues that sports analytics tracks load, sleep and heart rate variability but almost never tracks hormonal physiology. She says the menstrual cycle should be treated as a measurable signal, not noise, and that female athletes' higher rates of ACL and bone stress injuries come from hormonal, structural and environmental factors together. She reports that average cycle-phase effects on performance are small while individual effects can be large, and that calendar counting misses anovulation and luteal phase defects. She proposes a practical framework: symptom tracking, screening, a composite score, and athlete education, with attention to data privacy.

## Key claims

- Hormonal physiology is rarely tracked in sports, unlike load, GPS, HRV and sleep [00:39].
- In an audit of top exercise science and sports medicine journals, only 6% of the research used female-specific data [04:50].
- Female athletes have higher injury rates for bone stress injuries, ACL injuries and concussions, and these are predictable patterns [05:51].
- She frames the cycle as an algorithm of dynamic hormonal signaling, not a calendar [06:22].
- Not every athlete who bleeds has a regular cycle: hormonal contraception, luteal phase defects, anovulation and irregular bleeds are possible, and calendar tracking cannot detect them [07:55].
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews conclude that average phase effects on performance are trivial or small, but individual effects can be large [08:27].
- The field is moving from phase-based prescription and "cycle syncing" toward individualized monitoring [08:59].
- Symptom burden may affect performance more than the hormonal impact itself [09:30].
- ACL fibers contain receptors for estrogen, progesterone and relaxin, and knee laxity changes across the cycle, but there is no conclusive evidence on how hormone fluctuations affect ACL injury risk [10:32].
- Anatomical and biomechanical factors (femoral notch, tibial slope, landing patterns, alignment, quad dominance) interact with hormonal ones [11:03].
- Female teams often have less medical and strength staffing and more reactive care than male teams [11:34].
- She proposes a multilevel risk framework: athlete, team, equipment, organization and society [12:04].
- Low energy availability can suppress estrogen, cause missed periods, lower bone mineral density and raise bone stress injury risk; RED-S and the female athlete triad are the clinical models [13:38], [14:08].
- Calendar counting assumes a 28-day cycle, but a normal cycle can be 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- Blood testing is invasive and expensive, urinary testing needs frequent samples, and wearables still need validation in athlete settings [15:42].
- Her implementation framework is symptom tracking, RED-S and ACL screening, wearable data, a composite score used to adjust load, recovery, nutrition and hydration, and education of athletes and staff [16:46], [17:17].
- She wants the menstrual cycle treated as a vital sign for every female athlete [17:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 6% of journal research was female-specific; 94% male or mixed [04:50].
- ACL injury annual rate "almost 4%" in certain sports versus 0.03% in the general population [10:01].
- Normal cycle length 21 to 35 days [15:12].
- "One in five of natural cycles in some populations" can have chronic or spontaneous anovulation [15:12].
- Rehabilitation after ACL surgery: 9 to 12 months [03:17].
- Bone mineral density described as accounting for 50 to 70% of variation in bone strength [14:39]. Caption reads "accounts to 4 50 to 70%", so the number is partly garbled.
- Female athlete triad: low energy availability, impaired menstrual cycle, impaired bone health [14:08].
- Eumenorrheic: a regular menstrual cycle [07:24].
- Participation remark in Q&A: "50% or less" collecting data is a poor situation [20:01]; the caption is garbled.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Multilevel risk framework (individual, team and equipment, society and organization) [12:04].
- RED-S and female athlete triad as screening models [14:08].
- Gold-standard cycle measurement: serologic testing, quantitative urinary hormone testing, wearables [15:42].
- Proposed composite score from symptoms, screens and wearable data [16:46].

## Limits and open questions

- She says evidence on phase effects and ACL risk is limited, mixed or inconclusive [08:59], [10:32].
- No sample sizes, effect sizes or study citations are given for the performance claims.
- The composite score is proposed, not shown or validated.
- The framework has not been shown to reduce injuries; "predictable so preventable" is her stated belief [05:51], [18:19].
- Wearable validation in athletes is acknowledged as incomplete [15:42].
- The session description cites 2 to 8 times ACL rates and 2 to 4 times bone stress rates; those figures are not stated in the captions.

## Q&A

- How to convince organizations to invest: athletes are asking for it; include athletes; introduce in the off-season; low participation undermines it [19:29], [20:01].
- Advice for youth and under-resourced settings: start the conversation at the start of the season, keep it simple, use handouts and videos, have athletes track in a phone or journal [21:03], [22:03].
- Personalizing without a blanket solution: slight tweaks rather than individual programs; strength training as foundation [23:40], [24:10].
- Using data to optimize as well as prevent: tracking can show when an athlete feels best [25:12].
- Privacy and opt-in: athlete owns and controls her data; data must not be used to pull athletes from play [26:43].

speakers: [CJ LaBoy, Arun Batra Kora (caption spelling), Dan Murphy, Kayla Jennings, Warren Zola (moderator)]
topics: [policy, front-office, decision-making, american-football, basketball]
confidence: untested

## Summary

A panel of an agency football executive, a football and NIL manager, an ESPN reporter, a basketball marketing director and a moderator discusses how NIL, revenue sharing and agents have changed college athletes' decisions to stay, transfer or turn pro. Panelists say recruiting now starts earlier, agent activity is unregulated and sometimes predatory, and NIL Go review is unworkable. They say staying in school can pay more than turning pro for some athletes, especially in women's sports. They call for agent certification, collective bargaining, and separate treatment of top-tier programs. Most claims are opinion and experience, not data.

## Key claims

- Dan Murphy says most college athletes are better off than a decade ago and expects one more stage where the top end splits from the rest of the NCAA [05:09].
- Murphy says the current system does not work well for anyone involved [05:39].
- CJ LaBoy says recruiting profiles have not changed but recruiting now reaches freshmen and sophomores in high school [06:39], [07:10].
- LaBoy says the recruiting process is cloudier and less transparent than ever at the top end [08:13].
- Another panelist says first-mover agents approach athletes early and expects the market to mature as athletes share stories [09:44], [10:14].
- Murphy says groups have signed 16- and 17-year-olds to deals that resemble loans, and says regulation limiting contract length for minors could help [12:46], [13:16].
- Panelists favor agent certification, and one suggests a collective bargaining agreement even if unofficial [15:19], [16:51].
- A panelist says no school is honest about what it pays players [17:21].
- The moderator says the NCAA and Deloitte created NIL Go for deals over $600 [18:24].
- Kayla Jennings says her firm treats NIL Go as a must and brands ask to submit deals early [19:27].

## Summary

Four athletes and coaches plus a moderator discuss how elite performers reach and keep peak performance. Panelists say they wish they had mental tools and recovery planning earlier, and that modern athletes start professional habits early. A recurring theme is the constraints-led approach: Epstein, whose book is about constraints, and others describe removing the usual solution so that athletes or teams explore new ones. The discussion is built on personal stories, with a few cited studies described from memory. Closing views are that AI will help, but the bottleneck is turning data into action.

## Key claims

- Battier says he wishes he had mental-health tools; he now teaches teenagers breathing [02:38], [03:09].
- Murphy says he wishes he had perspective, and that how he felt in warm-up did not predict race outcome [03:40].
- Magness tells of a sports psychologist who said knitting helped a driven athlete by balancing the rest of her life [05:12], [05:42].
- Epstein says he did not program recovery like training and improved when he dropped one workout a week late in his career [07:13].
- Murphy says his approach moves from working harder, to nutrition, recovery, physical therapy and mental strategies, tried well before competition [08:13], [09:15].
- Battier says top young players now have workout, basketball and mental coaches in high school and arrive already professional [10:16], [10:48].
- Magness says achieving and sustaining are different: a 15-year-old can look good on pro methods and fade by 18 to 20 because foundations were skipped [11:48], [12:20], [12:52].
- Epstein cites a Science paper on 30,000 careers, saying world-class adults were almost entirely different people from the best kids, and some predictors of youth success were negative predictors of adult success [13:54].
- Murphy says his college coach built belief step by step and he finished fourth at trials in the 200 back [16:26], [17:28].
- Battier says great coaches spent time figuring him out, and Coach K promised only the chance to earn playing time [19:00].
- Epstein describes constraints as blocking the usual solution to force exploration; brains default to the path of least resistance [24:31].
- Epstein cites a study of pass networks in 30,000 NBA games where teammates spread the ball when a star was out and kept some of it on his return [22:31], [23:01].
- Epstein says the sprint start accounts for 50% of variance in skeleton finish time, and a Canadian coach's instruction to do anything but the usual led to a one-handed start [23:31], [24:01].
- Epstein says people keep self-interrupting at their accustomed rate after distractions are removed, so focus must be trained [22:01].
- Murphy says the Olympics are not an optimal environment, so his team schedules the day in 15-minute increments to remove thinking under pressure [25:33], [26:34].
- Magness says he taped off a soccer field as a warm-up area so an athlete must adapt to a long wait; Tom Tellez had him run barefoot and use mini hurdles to change a pattern he could not feel [27:35], [29:06], [29:36].
- Battier says rebuilding his jump shot took months of one-handed shooting close to the rim [31:36], [32:06].
- Magness says Tellez switched Carl Lewis's takeoff leg and the trust built by a good reason mattered [33:38].
- Epstein tells of Sheila Taormina using a theory-of-constraints bottleneck audit to reach four Olympics in three sports [35:11], [35:42].
- Murphy says multiple sources of motivation and a strong training group help consistency [37:15], [37:45].
- Epstein says Bears GM Ryan Poles turned six draft picks into 11 by trading back; Tony Fadell advises writing the press release first as a bounding box [38:46], [39:17], [40:18].
- Magness says everyday athletes should set the bar by their actual goal, and cites a 1970s marathon study: novices used one strategy, elite marathoners about 15 [41:48], [42:18], [42:50].
- Next big thing: Epstein, AI video prediction [43:54], [44:24]; Battier, performing under pressure [44:54]; Murphy, AI spotting motivation dips [45:24]; Magness, communicating actionable insight from tracked data [45:56], [46:28].

## Numbers and definitions

- Battier played 13 years in the NBA [02:38].
- Magness ran a 4:01 mile [04:10].
- 30,000 careers in the Science paper [13:54]; 30,000 NBA games in the pass-network study [22:31].
- Murphy was about 15th in the US at 16 before the 2012 Olympics and finished fourth at trials in the 200 back (top two make the team) [15:56], [16:26], [17:28].

## Limits and open questions

## Summary

A panel from the NCAA, a data vendor, Ticketmaster and South Carolina athletics discusses using data to grow college sports revenue as the House settlement raises costs. Panelists describe collecting fan data across NCAA events, segmenting fans for marketing, annual ticket price increases, dynamic pricing and a unified secondary market. They describe AI as accelerating discovery and letting non-coders query data, with humans in the loop. Results are self-reported by panelists with commercial or institutional interests. The panel is about revenue and fan data, not athlete performance data.

- The moderator says the House settlement introduced annual revenue sharing of 20 million and back pay of almost three billion, so institutions must generate revenue [01:34].
- Brian Higgins says men's basketball is about 80% of NCAA revenue and the NCAA runs 94 championships [03:08].
- Higgins says the NCAA wants to collect every piece of fan data it legally can, from ticket partners, streams and brackets [04:08].
- Kelly says NCAA championships will touch 46 states, over 170 events and 1.1 million customers this year [05:10].
- Picaduro says pricing has shifted from setting a price and hoping to intentional strategy, with college catching up to pro [07:12], [07:43].
